lead: This unit builds the mathematical language behind quantum computing: complex vectors, Hilbert spaces, matrices, Hermitian and unitary operators, tensor products and operator functions. It starts with why quantum computing exists and ends with the tools to write a quantum state and a quantum gate. After it you can read a qubit as a unit vector and a gate as a unitary matrix.
about: 1.1 sets the scene: why quantum computing exists, what changed from classical computing, and where the field is going. 1.2 builds complex numbers and vector spaces, the raw material for quantum states. 1.3 adds inner products and Dirac notation, so a state becomes a ket in a Hilbert space. 1.4 turns matrices into linear operators and finds eigenvalues and eigenvectors. 1.5 studies Hermitian and unitary matrices, the two classes that describe measurement and gates. 1.6 combines small spaces into composite systems with tensor products. 1.7 defines functions of operators, including the matrix exponential used for time evolution and gates.

chapters.idea: Quantum computing trades classical bits for a different physical model of information, and its history shows why that trade is hard and valuable.
chapters.depth: High-level story only: Feynman 1982 on simulating physics, BB84 1984 for secure key distribution, Deutsch 1985 on a universal quantum computer, Shor 1994 on factoring, Grover 1996 on search. Explain why a classical bit is 0 or 1 while a qubit is a unit vector in C² (details in Unit 2). Compare classical and quantum computation by resources: bits, gates, measurement, interference, entanglement. List future directions: better qubits, error correction, scaling, algorithms, applications. Some syllabi call this introduction to quantum computing or quantum computation and quantum information.

figure.aria: A timeline places Feynman in 1982–1985, BB84 in 1984–1994, Deutsch in 1985–1994, Shor in 1994–1996 and Grover in 1996–2000 on three lanes.

chapters.example: Question: A 50-qubit state has how many amplitudes? At 16 bytes per amplitude, how much memory is needed? Answer: 2⁵⁰ ≈ 1.126×10¹⁵ amplitudes; 1.126×10¹⁵ × 16 bytes ≈ 1.8×10¹⁶ bytes = 18 PB (1 PB = 10¹⁵ bytes). This is one reason classical simulation of many qubits is hard.
chapters.trap: Do not say a quantum computer checks all 2ⁿ answers and returns the best one. Amplitudes can cancel, and measurement gives one outcome with probabilities.
chapters.leave: Qubit representation, Bloch sphere, postulates, measurement, gates, circuits and algorithms go to Units 2–4.

chapters.idea: A vector space over the complex numbers gives the stage on which quantum states are built.
chapters.depth: Complex numbers as a+bi with a,b real; i²=−1; conjugate a−bi; modulus; polar form r(cosθ+i sinθ)=re^{iθ}; arithmetic. Vector space over C: scalars are complex; axioms; examples Cⁿ; linear combination, span, linear independence, basis, dimension. Keep inner products for the next chapter. Some syllabi call this review of linear algebra.

figure.title: w equals i times v
figure.aria: The table shows v = (1, i), w = (i, −1), and the row i·v equals w, so the two vectors are dependent over C.

chapters.example: In C², take v=(1,i) and w=(i,−1). Are they linearly independent over C? Try w=cv: the first coordinate gives c=i; then c·i=i²=−1, which matches the second coordinate. So w=i·v and the set is dependent.
chapters.trap: Linear independence must use complex scalars. Two vectors can look independent over real numbers but be dependent over C.
chapters.leave: Inner products, norms and Dirac notation go to 1.3; matrix operators go to 1.4.

chapters.idea: An inner product turns a complex vector space into a Hilbert space, and Dirac notation writes vectors and inner products compactly.
chapters.depth: Inner product on a complex vector space: ⟨φ|ψ⟩; conjugate symmetry ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩*; linear in the second argument; positive definite. Norm ||ψ||=√⟨ψ|ψ⟩; orthogonality; orthonormal basis; completeness Σᵢ|i⟩⟨i|=I. Hilbert space as a complete inner product space; finite-dimensional Cⁿ is enough here. Dirac notation: ket |ψ⟩ as a column vector, bra ⟨ψ| as a conjugate row, dual correspondence, inner product bracket. Computational basis |0⟩, |1⟩. Some syllabi call this Hilbert spaces and Dirac notation.

figure.aria: A ket passes to its bra, then pairs with |0⟩ and with itself to give the coefficient and the norm from the example.

chapters.trap: The bra is the conjugate transpose, not just the transpose. Reversing the order gives the complex conjugate: ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩*.
chapters.leave: Operators and matrices go to 1.4; qubit measurement goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A linear operator is a matrix once a basis is chosen, and its eigenvalues and eigenvectors reveal its action.
chapters.depth: Linear operator A: A(αu+βv)=αAu+βAv. Matrix of A in a basis; addition, scalar multiplication, composition as matrix product; identity and inverse; determinant. Eigenvalue equation Av=λv; characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0; eigenvectors; diagonalization when there are enough independent eigenvectors. Use 2×2 examples only. Pauli matrices appear as operators, but their quantum meaning is in Unit 2 and Unit 3. Some syllabi call this matrices and operators.

figure.aria: The operator A splits into eigenvalue 3 with eigenvector (1, 1) and eigenvalue 1 with eigenvector (1, −1).

chapters.example: For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], det(A−λI)=(2−λ)²−1=λ²−4λ+3=(λ−3)(λ−1). Eigenvalues are 3 and 1. Eigenvectors: for λ=3, (1,1); for λ=1, (1,−1).
chapters.trap: Eigenvectors are nonzero. Do not solve Av=λv by dividing by v; write (A−λI)v=0 and force det(A−λI)=0.
chapters.leave: Hermitian and unitary special classes go to 1.5; Pauli gate actions go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Hermitian matrices describe observables, and unitary matrices describe reversible gates and time evolution.
chapters.depth: Conjugate transpose A†=(A*)ᵀ. Hermitian A=A†; unitary U†U=UU†=I. Hermitian: real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors, spectral decomposition A=Σλ|λ⟩⟨λ|. Unitary: preserves inner product and norm, eigenvalues have modulus 1, U⁻¹=U†. Examples: Pauli X, Y, Z are Hermitian and unitary; Hadamard H is Hermitian and unitary. Some syllabi call this Hermitian and unitary matrices.

figure.aria: The Hadamard matrix equals its conjugate transpose, and its square is the identity, giving the Hermitian and unitary checks.

chapters.trap: Hermitian and unitary are different tests. A real symmetric matrix is Hermitian but may not be unitary; a unitary matrix need not be Hermitian.
chapters.leave: Measurement postulates and gate circuits go to Units 2 and 3.

chapters.idea: The tensor product builds the state space of a composite quantum system from the state spaces of its parts.
chapters.depth: Tensor product of vector spaces V⊗W: bilinear, dimension dimV·dimW, basis |i⟩⊗|j⟩ written |ij⟩. Kronecker product for matrices; operators A⊗B act on the product basis. Composite systems: two qubits live in C²⊗C² with basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. Keep entanglement and measurement for Unit 2. Some syllabi call this tensor products.

figure.title: Basis of C² ⊗ C²
figure.aria: A two-by-two table lists the four product basis states |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩ and |11⟩.

chapters.trap: Dimension multiplies, not adds. Order matters: |0⟩⊗|1⟩=|01⟩ is not |10⟩=|1⟩⊗|0⟩.
chapters.leave: Entanglement, Bell states and CNOT go to Units 2 and 3.

chapters.idea: A function of an operator is defined through its eigenvalues, and the matrix exponential gives unitary time evolution.
chapters.depth: Functions of an operator: powers, polynomials, power series. For a Hermitian (or normal) A with spectral decomposition A=Σλ|λ⟩⟨λ|, define f(A)=Σf(λ)|λ⟩⟨λ|. Matrix exponential e^A=Σ Aᵏ/k!; unitary time evolution U=e^{−iHt/ħ} for Hermitian H and real t. Use diagonal examples to compute quickly. Some syllabi call this operator functions.

figure.aria: A diagonal operator A goes to its spectral form, then f(A), then e^{iA}, giving diag(1, −1).

chapters.example: Let A=diag(0,π). Then e^{iA}=diag(e^{i0},e^{iπ})=diag(1,−1). Check: e^{iA} is unitary because its eigenvalues 1 and −1 have modulus 1.
chapters.trap: Do not apply the function entry by entry to a general matrix. Apply it to eigenvalues in the spectral form; only diagonal matrices allow entry-by-entry.
chapters.leave: Hamiltonian dynamics and algorithm phases go to Units 2–4; exponential gates go to Unit 3.
